Breaking: The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece.
  • All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years.
  • Sources indicate that our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Sources indicate that our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Debuted in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

In a recent development, I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

In a recent development, much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Launched in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

When I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

Imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Debuted in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere new—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Recent findings suggest that terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

According to recent reports, this was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Debuted in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

According to recent reports, I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Debuted in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still confirms itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

Industry observers note that it came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Debuted in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

In a recent development, halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Launched in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Industry observers note that amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Rolled out in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating).

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

It has been revealed that heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

According to recent reports, to a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

In a recent development, to a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

Tech Report: Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • Industry observers note that it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

Industry observers note that it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

It has been revealed that while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

In a recent development, but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of deals, but they play a little differently. Significant-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#203526. Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2279 w)

Nature on the Board: Should Brands Opt In?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa.
  • Recent findings suggest that for 50 years, natural beauty manufacturer Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’.
  • Enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

Recent findings suggest that for 50 years, natural beauty manufacturer Faith In Nature has been guided by the slogan ‘nature is the boss’. It was plastered on the office walls and repeated ad nauseam by staff, but had no legal footing. Then, in 2021, creative directors Simeon Rose and Anne Hopkins put the provocation to a group of groundbreaking legal experts: how could they turn the slogan into something more?

Enter Nature on the Board (NOTB), a growing global movement where companies appoint a proxy for nature to their board of directors, recognizing and advocating for the rights of nature in decision-making processes, and flipping traditional corporate governance on its head. Some companies appoint a nature director — a human proxy for nature, who holds a formal board seat, written into the organization’s articles of association, with the same financial and legal duties as other board members. Others appoint nature guardians, who perform a similar role in advocating for nature at the board level, but they don’t necessarily have voting rights.

A new programme by Kering and the Centre for Sustainable Fashion hopes to reimagine how companies make high-level decisions, but is the industry ready to embrace change?

NOTB was proposed by Faith In Nature, and fleshed out by legal non-profits Lawyers for Nature and the Earth Law Center (ELC), but it was inspired by Indigenous communities who have practiced nature-centric governance for millennia. “The current business system is operating exactly as it was designed to: businesses pool capital, build goods and services at scale, speed and low cost, and accrue benefits for shareholders,” explains Mary Johnstone-Louis, senior fellow in management at the University of Oxford’s Saïd Business School. “Putting nature on the board is radical because it introduces a stakeholder on which every business depends, but whose interests are not typically represented at the board level.”.

While there was no precedent for putting nature on the board, there were other case studies to draw on, says Lawyers for Nature co-founder and managing director Brontie Ansell. “Until relatively recently, women were seen as objects of law, rather than subjects of law. Like nature, they were not allowed to hold property, vote or voice concerns. Now, we look back on that with horror,” she explains. “Likewise, we are very familiar with widening the stakeholder pool in boardrooms. Many now include HR managers, union representatives, and health and safety officers. Extending this to nature is critical to human survival.”.

Alongside Faith In Nature, NOTB has since been adopted by dozens of companies, including British interiors brand House of Hackney, Norwegian apparel brand Northern Playground, and French IT services manufacturer Norsys. Each has put their own spin on the blueprint, contributing to a fast-evolving consensus on best practices, and throwing open the doors for further innovation. Vogue Business invited these early adopters to share the tensions, toggles and opportunities.

Businesses are just as diverse and idiosyncratic as nature, indicates Faith In Nature managing director Hannah Whittaker. When it comes to putting nature on the board, each business has to do it in its own way.

NOTB encourages companies to give nature voting rights, but it’s possible to test nature governance without this. Outdoor apparel brand Patagonia made waves in 2022 when it created a nature purpose trust model, making a collection of environmental non-profits the beneficiary of 98% of its non-voting stock, while retaining approval rights in the Patagonia Purpose Trust, controlled by the family of founder Yvon Chouinard.

Approaches may also differ by jurisdiction, notes ELC’s nature governance business development associate Anna Solgaard, who acts as the nature guardian for Norwegian clothing label Northern Playground. Finding ways to give nature more legal rights requires “creative lawyering”, adds Alexandra Pimor, director of the ELC’s Nature Governance Agency. “That’s the beauty of nature on the board: we did not have to change the law to do it, we just changed our relationship with the law to give it a different purpose [taking existing rights for board members and extending them to nature]. In a capitalist environment, the corporate world is probably the easiest place to embed the voice of nature, because companies are given so much freedom.”.

At Norsys, nature is both a director and a shareholder with a 10% stake in the business. “This is a strong model because it means nature will always be represented on the board, it’s not just one nomination we forget about in three years,” claims the company’s nature director Frantz Gault, author of Nature at Work and co-founder of Vivøices, a public interest organization promoting the representation of the living world in organizational governance. Gault helped design the nature governance at Norsys, complementing his own role with a council of advisors, who also decide how dividends from nature’s 10% stake are spent.

Lawyers for Nature, on the other hand, prefers for nature directors to remain as “conflict-free” as possible. In the frameworks it has designed, nature representatives are not heavily salaried by the company, they don’t have a bonus linked to profit, they don’t owe the company money or vice versa, and they don’t have — or at least, they commit to disclosing — any other conflicts of interest. “By minimizing those conflicts, the nature representative can speak in the purest form possible about what nature needs,” indicates Ansell.

At Northern Playground, the articles of association include a “safety valve” whereby the nature proxy can be relieved of their duties if the company is approaching bankruptcy, to reduce the risk of them being held personally liable.

According to recent reports, another contention point is whether the nature proxy should have the right to veto strategic decisions, as well as voting on them. “If you get to the point where you need a veto, you’ve already lost,” states Dr Juliet Rose, head of development at the British botanical garden and research hub The Eden Project, and nature director at Faith In Nature. “You’re trying to get everybody moving in the same direction, so nobody even suggests something that would require a veto.”.

At Norsys, Gault has the power to veto, but has never activated it. To keep the “nuclear power” in check, he is required to confer with a council of 10 scientific experts before taking a position in board meetings. Still, knowing the veto exists can be persuasive enough. “Everyone knows I have the power to veto, so the other directors listen when I speak, and they work with me to find a consensus.” If a veto isn’t on the cards, companies can implement the right to disagree, and the right to express that disagreement in public, adds Gault, or the right to resign. “These are little legal technicalities, but they help make nature’s voice more meaningful.”.

In a recent development, whichever approach a organization chooses, Vivøices recommends running a year-long pilot before codifying nature’s role or communicating the program to consumers. “You do a pilot, then map the impact and what happened, how it changed the way decisions were made, how it influenced the culture internally, and what it means to really integrate the position of nature,” states co-founder Niels de Fraguier.

Sources indicate that when House of Hackney advertised a directorship “for mother nature and future generations” in 2023, it received over 500 applications — its most popular job listing to date. But finding the right person to represent something as nebulous as nature was no small feat. “We had applications from scientists, teachers, poets and everything in between,” indicates House of Hackney co-founder Frieda Gormley, author of In the Manufacturer of Nature.

Sources indicate that the challenge is finding someone who can bridge economic and ecological realities, claims the University of Oxford’s Johnstone-Louis. “They have to protect the manufacturer, and at the same time, they have to speak for nature. That means they have to toggle between immediacy and long-termism; between business as usual and what business could be,” she says. Regardless of their professional background, humility and diplomacy are the key competencies, adds de Fraguier.

According to recent reports, both Faith In Nature and House of Hackney appointed Lawyers for Nature’s Ansell as their inaugural nature director, establishing the legal basis for the role and ironing out any kinks. Her successors have wildly different skill sets: Rose has a background in plant science and ecology, while House of Hackney’s nature director Charmian Love specializes in governance, having co-founded B Lab UK, the organization behind the B Corp certification. Love says her goal is to create tools that make it easier for more diverse nature proxies to step into the role in future, while Rose says her success is defined by how well she empowers staff throughout the tech giant, so whoever holds the nature directorship is not working alone, or resting solely on their own, inevitably limited, experience.

It has been revealed that ideally, nature-centric decision-making cascades down through the company, and the nature director works in tandem with a well-established nature lead. While the former stewards the long-term purpose of the business, the latter embeds it in day-to-day operations. Without a nature director in their corner, a nature lead can easily fall into the same trap as sustainability leads, tasked with overhauling the business but lacking the resource or buy-in to do so, instead operating in a silo and trying to shoehorn change into business as usual. And without a nature lead to operationalize nature-centric decision-making, a nature director risks becoming little more than “window dressing”, indicates Johnstone-Louis.

Industry observers note that to avoid tokenizing nature, Faith In Nature has designed a nature dashboard, which translates its goals into tangible projects each team can track progress against. Projects fall into five governing principles: governance, operational impact, sourcing, community and regeneration. “We had to work through the confusion and connect each team with the outcomes we wanted for nature, each of which has budgets, resources and KPIs attached,” explains Whittaker. “Otherwise, the concept can be quite theoretical for staff.” These projects span from changing the adhesive on labels to make at-home recycling easier, to running the brand’s first major television ad in collaboration with Channel 4 and B Corp.

Industry observers note that at House of Hackney, Love starts every board meeting with a nature degradation pulse-check and a poem about nature, based on climate policy leader Nigel Topping’s remarks that “we need to be guided by science and moved by poetry”. Beyond board meetings, Love has defined 10 topics that are material to nature, from supply chain and procurement to regulatory changes and financial investments. Decisions about these topics are automatically escalated to a monthly nature meeting. She has also introduced a spin on the traditional ‘going concern test’ boards use to assess how nature-related decisions will affect the company’s future viability and license to operate.

On top of this, Love has a private email address where staff can discreetly voice concerns or ideas, and the company regularly invites inspirational nature-related speakers into the office. The next phase is to trial a physical card game, she says, which will live in every meeting room, encouraging staff to question their daily decision-making through a nature-centric lens, inspired by similar games at tea brand Pukka Herbs. And at the end of the year, House of Hackney will publish an open-source toolkit for NOTB, informed by its Greenprint fellowship, where 10 SMEs — including Lush, Davines and Vivobarefoot — experimented with nature governance over 12 months.

NOTB is not just another sustainability box for companies to tick; it’s a paradigm shift that goes beyond sustainability, toward regeneration.

“Philosophically, these are two very different landscapes,” explains Solgaard. “Sustainability is an anthropocentric paradigm, but nature is ecocentric, which means that the more-than-human world is valued alongside humans. Sustainability works with separation and reductionism, which is why we have all these boxes to tick, and we struggle to view things holistically, or to see how everything is interconnected. Nature is everything.”.

In a recent development, putting nature on the board also means moving beyond the risk mitigation approach that has defined so many corporate nature strategies, and underscored the business case for nature, to date, adds Johnstone-Louis. The risk mitigation approach asks how companies can continue to extract resources like cotton and wool pulp from nature, and reduce supply chain disruption from nature-related disasters like water scarcity and flooding. The NOTB approach — especially for companies like House of Hackney, which have combined nature with future generations — asks how decisions made today will affect the ability of future systems to thrive, sometimes looking as far ahead as seven generations. “It’s a different way of seeing the world,” she adds.

In a recent development, addressing nature directly is a leap into the unknown — not least because so few companies have mapped their nature risks and dependencies. But rather than face this with fear, Pimor encourages companies to see the opportunities. “We are facing the most incredible, unprecedented ecological challenge. Facing the unknown means becoming more open to creativity, innovation and imagination. That’s what the voice of nature brings to the table.”.

Deep transformation tends to be slow and steady, concludes Ansell. “Slow isn’t ideal in the situation we find ourselves in, but it’s better than going backwards. The idea here is for nature to be a gentle guiding voice, moving the rudder one degree at a time until the ship has completely changed course. It’s exciting. There’s so much still up for grabs in terms of distilling the theory and making it work for each individual sector or situation.”.

In a recent development, A major, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you blueprint to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

In a recent development, we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

According to recent reports, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Recent findings suggest that let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too swiftly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Industry observers note that bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Industry observers note that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

It has been revealed that transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

All told, the GN70-K is best for the person who just needs a dependable nose and ear trimmer that will save them from the mess. Adam Hurly.

A whole grooming kit is excessive if all you need to tackle is the occasional nose hair. But if you’re also maintaining a beard, tidying body hair, or cutting your own hair, Philips’ 9000 starts to make much more sense. The current kit has 23 tools and accessories, including a nose and ear head, with a stainless-steel handle and rubber grip. Philips rates it for up to six hours between charges.

Long-term testing notes: Philips' previous iteration of the Multigroom 9000 was my go-to grooming tool. Alas, I only realized how much I relied on its nose hair shaving attachment after I lost the thing. Now there's a new (albeit broadly similar) update of the same device, and I'm back to trimming as much hair as humanly possible with one device. My advice for anyone else who picks up this trimmer? Be sure to check every piece when packing up after a trip. Adam Hurly.

My nose hairs have become alarmingly ambitious with age, which is unfortunate given how little enthusiasm I have for plucking, waxing, or the local Turkish barber’s fire tricks. The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro, thankfully, gets the job done with considerably less drama. Alongside its rotary nose and ear head, there’s a separate eyebrow blade with a 2mm comb. USB-C charging saves another proprietary cable, and the travel lock stops it switching on in your bag.

Recent findings suggest that long-term testing notes: During my review testing, the rotary head cut through my thick, wiry hairs promptly, without the pulling and sneezing fits I’ve experienced with cheaper trimmers. It was still ticklish, but the compact head was easy to maneuver around my nostrils and ears. The LED helped in my dimly lit bathroom, showing hairs I might otherwise have missed. I also liked the solid-feeling matte-black handle and how easily it rinsed clean. The claimed hour of runtime held up in testing, too. It’s the best dedicated nose trimmer I’ve used. Esat Dedezade.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a beard and your grooming routine requires a more exacting tool, ConairMan’s Nose and Ear Trimmer kit will serve you well. I think of this more as a mustache and beard-line tidier-upper, as opposed to a nose hair trimmer.

The tool has a rotary blade that makes quick work of nostril hairs. But its two-faced trimming and shaving head is its best calling card—you get a straight-edge detailer on one side, and a shaver on the other. If you’re looking for a tool that can truly tend to the lower half of your face, ConairMan offers an excellent package that’ll get the job done. Adam Hurly.

In a recent development, philips’ 7000 costs less than the 9000 above and still covers far more than nose hair. The US kit includes 22 tools and accessories, with a precision comb for short facial hair and heads for wider grooming jobs. Finding somewhere to keep all those small parts is part of the deal.

My main complaint, as always, is the proprietary charging connection. The supplied cable plugs into USB-A at the other end, but you still need Philips’ cable to charge the trimmer. Braun, Remington, and other brands are just as guilty of this, by the way.

Industry observers note that long-term testing notes: In my three-week test of the 7000, its nose and ear attachment cut comfortably without pulling, snagging, or irritation. It was much less unpleasant than plucking. The wider kit also earned its place on my chest and underarms, so the extra attachments felt useful. Esat Dedezade.

Industry observers note that if you already have a Panasonic MultiShape, the nose-trimming head gives its rechargeable handle another job. It swaps with the system’s beard trimmer, shaver, and toothbrush heads, so there’s one less complete gadget to pack when you travel.

Industry observers note that for a new buyer, the lithium-ion handle and nose head cost around $81.99 together. The $21.99 attachment won’t work on its own, and the other heads cost extra. That makes the MultiShape easier to justify if you’ll use more of the system. For nose hair alone, a dedicated trimmer is a simpler buy.

Industry observers note that long-term testing notes: During several weeks with a broader MultiShape kit, I found the nose head cleared unwanted hair without pain or friction. The lightweight handle was comfortable, and switching from trimming to shaving or brushing his teeth took little effort. That ease of moving between jobs made the system particularly useful for travel. The handle and nose head linked here are sold separately from the other attachments he used. Owen Gough.

Recent findings suggest that while many nose hair trimmers tout motors with serious RPMs and boast about their long battery life, the truth is, you won’t be using it much—maybe once every couple weeks for a mere 5 or 10 seconds. But that’s no excuse to skimp on them, either. Here are a few things to consider:.

We’ve tested all manner of nose hair trimmers for this guide, from simple battery-powered models to grooming kits with interchangeable heads. We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

Recent findings suggest that the guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. You can read more about our editorial standards at About GQ.

What is the best nose hair trimmer?

The best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Can a nose hair trimmer cut you?

It has been revealed that whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is important to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

How do you use a nose hair trimmer?

To trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:.

How do I clean my nose hair trimmer?

The cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” says Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more key that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”.

Simone (who is professionally mononymous) is a celebrity men’s groomer. Her A-List clients include Mahershala Ali, Ramy Youssef, Jason Schwartzman, John Magaro, and Brandon Perea.

Adam Hurly has been covering men's grooming for GQ since 2016. He also writes about travel. Adam is a Sioux Falls, SD native, University of Kansas graduate, former Newly introduced Yorker, and current expat in Berlin. His favorite season is Oscar Season, his favorite book is Dinner At the Homesick Restaurant, and he is a proud superfan of Survivor.

Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better?
  • Industry observers note that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
  • 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so initiative ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

In a recent development, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

In a recent development, place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

The bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.
